claim: Cryo-EM reconstructions of no-nucleotide and ATP analog-bound kinesin-microtubule complexes were obtained at 5-6 Å resolution.
source: Through the application of recent advances in instrumentation and image processing, including the use of a high-speed electron-counting detector and algorithms to correct for beam-induced sample motion (Li et al., 2013) (See 'Materials and methods'), we were able to obtain a resolution of ∼5–6 Å in both of these maps (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B), a significant increase over previous studies of the kinesin-microtubule complex (Sindelar, 2011; Atherton et al., 2014; Goulet et al., 2014).
evidence: The resolution is directly stated and supported by FSC curves shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B, which are experimental measurements from the cryo-EM data.

claim: In some regions of the cryo-EM maps, the pitch of α-helices was resolved as were individual beta strands, indicating a resolution of at least 5 Å.
source: In some regions of the maps, the pitch of α-helices was resolved as were individual beta strands, indicating a resolution of at least 5 Å (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F,G).
evidence: The claim is supported by visual features in the density maps shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F,G.

claim: Binding of ATP analog causes the N-terminal subdomain to make a ~22° seesaw-like motion atop the lower subdomain.
source: In contrast, the N-terminal subdomain makes a ∼22° seesaw-like motion atop the lower subdomain (compare Figure 2A,B to Figure 2D,E) in response to binding of the ATP.
evidence: The motion is quantified from comparison of the two cryo-EM structures shown in Figure 2.

claim: In the ATP analog state, density consistent with a docked conformation of the neck linker extending towards the microtubule plus end was observed.
source: Correspondingly, in the ATP analog state, we observed density consistent with a docked conformation of the neck linker, extending towards the microtubule plus end (Figure 1B; Figure 2A,B), while in the no-nucleotide state the neck linker was evidently disordered (Figure 1B; Figure 2D,E), consistent with previous observations (Rice et al., 1999; Sindelar and Downing, 2007, 2010).
evidence: The observation is directly from the cryo-EM density maps shown in Figure 1B and Figure 2A,B, and is consistent with prior published observations.

claim: In the no-nucleotide state, the neck linker was disordered.
source: Correspondingly, in the ATP analog state, we observed density consistent with a docked conformation of the neck linker, extending towards the microtubule plus end (Figure 1B; Figure 2A,B), while in the no-nucleotide state the neck linker was evidently disordered (Figure 1B; Figure 2D,E), consistent with previous observations (Rice et al., 1999; Sindelar and Downing, 2007, 2010).
evidence: The observation is from the cryo-EM density maps and is consistent with previous studies.

claim: The upper subdomain rotates by ~11° in response to ATP binding.
source: Rigid-body fitting experiments using fragments of kinesin X-ray structures indicate that the upper subdomain rotates by much less (∼11°) than the N-terminal subdomain (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: The rotation angle is determined from rigid-body fitting experiments using the cryo-EM data.

claim: Both no-nucleotide and ATP analog-bound cryo-EM maps exhibit a contact between the switch II loop and switch II helix.
source: Related to this observation, we discovered a striking resemblance in the conformation of the switch II loop before and after binding of the ATP analog (Figure 2C,F; Figure 3). Both of our maps exhibit a contact between the switch II loop and switch II helix, coinciding with a pair of hydrogen bonds formed between the backbone of E236 and the side chain of N255 (respectively) in X-ray structures of kinesin's ATP analog-bound state (Parke et al., 2010; Chang et al., 2013; Gigant et al., 2013) (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: The contact is observed in both cryo-EM maps and corresponds to hydrogen bonds seen in X-ray structures.

claim: The cryo-EM maps resolve a contact between the switch II helix and the microtubule surface, corresponding to a hydrogen bond between N255 and M413 of alpha tubulin.
source: Proximal to this contact, our maps resolve another contact between the switch II helix and the microtubule surface, corresponding to a hydrogen bond between N255 and M413 of alpha tubulin in the kinesin–tubulin co-complex structure (Gigant et al., 2013).
evidence: The contact is resolved in the cryo-EM maps and corresponds to a hydrogen bond in the X-ray structure.

claim: In the no-nucleotide map, there is a distinct upward displacement of the P-loop away from the switch II loop.
source: A striking difference between our cryo-EM maps, however, is a distinct upward displacement of the P-loop away from the switch II loop in our no-nucleotide map.
evidence: The displacement is observed by comparing the two cryo-EM maps.

claim: The P-loop displacement appears to be a direct consequence of the 22° rotation made by the N-terminal subdomain.
source: This movement appears to be a direct consequence of the 22° rotation made by the N-terminal subdomain, to which the P-loop is anchored; the rotation translates the P-loop site ∼4 Å away from the microtubule surface.
evidence: The interpretation is based on the structural relationship between the N-terminal subdomain rotation and P-loop position observed in the cryo-EM data.

claim: The P-loop forms a visible contact with the switch II loop in the ATP analog map.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, while the P-loop forms a visible contact with the switch II loop in our ATP analog map (Figure 3B), a gap appears between these elements in the no-nucleotide map (Figure 3A).
evidence: The contact is visible in the cryo-EM density shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A gap appears between the P-loop and switch II loop in the no-nucleotide map.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, while the P-loop forms a visible contact with the switch II loop in our ATP analog map (Figure 3B), a gap appears between these elements in the no-nucleotide map (Figure 3A).
evidence: The gap is visible in the cryo-EM density shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In ADP-bound X-ray structures of kinesin, the P-loop and switch II loop maintain very close contact.
source: In contrast, the P-loop and switch II loop maintain very close contact in ADP-bound X-ray structures of kinesin (Figure 3C,D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: The observation is from X-ray crystal structures shown in the figures.

claim: In ADP-bound X-ray structures, the switch II loop fails to make close contact with the switch II helix.
source: At the same time, however, the switch II loop fails to make close contact with the switch II helix in the ADP-bound X-ray structures (Figure 3C,D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: The observation is from X-ray crystal structures shown in the figures.

claim: The conformation of kinesin visualized in the 4HNA structure is largely conserved when tubulin is incorporated into the microtubule lattice.
source: The MDFF calculation thus indicates that the conformation of kinesin visualized in the 4HNA structure is largely conserved when tubulin is incorporated into the microtubule lattice.
evidence: The conclusion is based on MDFF simulations that show only 1.08 Å backbone RMSD between the fitted structure and 4HNA.

claim: The switch loops remain 'closed' in an identical hydrogen-bonding network in both no-nucleotide and ATP states.
source: Remarkably, the switch loops remain 'closed' in an identical hydrogen-bonding network in our structural models for both nucleotide states.
evidence: The observation is from the atomic models derived from MDFF simulations of both cryo-EM maps.

claim: The hydrogen bond network that maintains closed switch loops includes a universally conserved salt bridge between R203 (switch I) and E236 (switch II).
source: The hydrogen bond partners in this network, which are shared by the 4HNA starting model, extend beyond the switch loops and include not only a universally conserved salt bridge between R203 (switch I) and E236 (switch II), but also several universally conserved residues in the switch II helix (E250, N255) and L7 from the upper subdomain (Y138) (Figure 4, middle and lower panels).
evidence: The hydrogen bond network is identified in the atomic models shown in Figure 4.

claim: Opening of the nucleotide cleft in the no-nucleotide model breaks a bifurcated hydrogen bond between T92 at the base of the P-loop and S202/D231 in switches I and II.
source: As the P-loop pulls away from the switch loops, a bifurcated hydrogen bond breaks up between T92 at the base of the P-loop and S202/D231 in switches I and II (Figure 4A,B and Video 3).
evidence: The hydrogen bond breaking is observed in the MDFF simulation trajectory shown in Video 3 and Figure 4.

claim: In the nucleotide-free structure, K91 breaks two hydrogen bonds with backbone carbonyl oxygens within the P-loop and swivels to interact with D231 in switch II.
source: In the nucleotide-free structure, K91 breaks two hydrogen bonds with a pair of backbone carbonyl oxygens within the interior of the P-loop and swivels around to interact with D231 in switch II, replacing the hydrogen bond this latter residue formerly made with T92.
evidence: The conformational change is observed in the no-nucleotide atomic model derived from MDFF.

claim: The side chain configuration within the active site of the nucleotide-free kinesin model is strikingly similar to nucleotide-free F1-ATPase and myosin motors.
source: The resulting side chain configuration within the active site of our nucleotide-free kinesin model is strikingly similar to what is seen in X-ray structures of nucleotide-free F1-ATPase and myosin motors, which possess homologous active-site architectures (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The similarity is demonstrated by comparison with X-ray structures shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both ADP-bound X-ray structures (1BG2 and 1MKJ) are prohibited from assuming favorable binding orientations on the microtubule surface due to the conformation of residue N255.
source: We discovered, however, that both the 1BG2 and 1MKJ structures are prohibited from assuming favorable binding orientations on the microtubule surface due to the conformation of residue N255.
evidence: The conclusion is based on structural comparison between ADP-bound X-ray structures and the microtubule-bound cryo-EM structures.

claim: The N-terminal coils of the switch II helix are unwound in both ADP-bound structures (1BG2 and 1MKJ).
source: As illustrated in Figure 4D–F, the N-terminal coils of the switch II helix are unwound in both ADP-bound structures.
evidence: The observation is from X-ray structures shown in Figure 4D-F.

claim: In ADP-bound structures, the peptide backbone at residue N255 would point directly at the H11–H12 loop of alpha tubulin, generating a substantial steric overlap.
source: Consequently, the peptide backbone at residue N255 would point directly at the H11–H12 loop of alpha tubulin, generating a substantial steric overlap (Figure 4F,I).
evidence: The steric clash is identified by modeling ADP-bound structures onto the microtubule surface as defined by the cryo-EM structures.

claim: The 1BG2 and 1MKJ conformations appear incapable of strong microtubule attachment, consistent with the weak experimentally observed microtubule affinity of kinesin's ADP state.
source: Thus, the 1BG2 and 1MKJ conformations appear incapable of strong microtubule attachment, consistent with the weak experimentally observed microtubule affinity of kinesin's ADP state (Rosenfeld et al., 1996).
evidence: The interpretation is based on structural analysis and is consistent with experimental measurements from the literature.

claim: The degree of end-to-end twisting in the no-nucleotide model falls within the range observed in other X-ray structures of ADP-bound kinesin.
source: In contrast to this expectation, however, we discovered that the degree of end-to-end twisting in both our no-nucleotide model as well as the previously reported 'rigor-like' ADP complex of KIF14 falls within the range observed in other X-ray structures of ADP-bound kinesin (Videos 4–6).
evidence: The comparison is made between the no-nucleotide model and multiple X-ray structures shown in Videos 4-6.

claim: ATP binding causes closure of the nucleotide cleft which is coupled to elastic strain in the peptide backbone, analogous to the action of an archery bow.
source: However, we identified another mode of distortion in our kinesin models, analogous to the action of an archery bow (Figure 6 and Videos 7,8), that would couple strong nucleotide binding to elastic strain in the peptide backbone.
evidence: The distortion mode is identified by comparing the no-nucleotide and ATP-bound models shown in Figure 6 and Videos 7-8.

claim: The N255K mutation reduces the rate of microtubule-stimulated ADP release by up to 1000-fold, to near basal levels.
source: Both of these predictions are supported by kinetics measurements reported here and elsewhere, which reveal that the N255K mutation reduces the rate of microtubule-stimulated ADP release by up to 1000-fold, to near basal levels (Auerbach and Johnson, 2005) (Figure 7A,B), while the E236A mutation increases the ADP off-rate of detached kinesin by 100-fold (Rice et al., 1999) but does not significantly alter the rate of microtubule-stimulated ADP release.
evidence: The claim is supported by kinetics measurements shown in Figure 7A,B and cited from Auerbach and Johnson, 2005.

claim: The E236A mutation increases the ADP off-rate of detached kinesin by 100-fold but does not significantly alter the rate of microtubule-stimulated ADP release.
source: Both of these predictions are supported by kinetics measurements reported here and elsewhere, which reveal that the N255K mutation reduces the rate of microtubule-stimulated ADP release by up to 1000-fold, to near basal levels (Auerbach and Johnson, 2005) (Figure 7A,B), while the E236A mutation increases the ADP off-rate of detached kinesin by 100-fold (Rice et al., 1999) but does not significantly alter the rate of microtubule-stimulated ADP release.
evidence: The claim is supported by kinetics measurements cited from Rice et al., 1999.

claim: Cryo-EM analysis of the N255K mutant reveals two previously unidentified binding modes in which the motor domain attaches tightly to the microtubule but is rotationally mobile.
source: Cryo-EM analysis of the ADP and ATP analog-bound states of the N255K point mutant of our construct support this hypothesis, revealing two previously unidentified binding modes of kinesin in which the motor domain attaches tightly to the microtubule but is rotationally mobile (Figure 7C–E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The binding modes are observed in cryo-EM reconstructions shown in Figure 7C-E.

claim: In the ADP-state map of N255K, the microtubule contact at site 255 appears to be attenuated or disordered.
source: In the ADP-state map, the microtubule contact at site 255 appears to be attenuated or disordered (Figure 7D, right panel), while in the AMPPNP map the wild-type microtubule contact of loop L12 is absent but a contact is evident at the 255 site (Figure 7E, right panel).
evidence: The observation is from the cryo-EM reconstruction shown in Figure 7D.

claim: In the AMPPNP map of N255K, the wild-type microtubule contact of loop L12 is absent but a contact is evident at the 255 site.
source: In the ADP-state map, the microtubule contact at site 255 appears to be attenuated or disordered (Figure 7D, right panel), while in the AMPPNP map the wild-type microtubule contact of loop L12 is absent but a contact is evident at the 255 site (Figure 7E, right panel).
evidence: The observation is from the cryo-EM reconstruction shown in Figure 7E.

claim: In neither nucleotide state is the N255K construct able to form all three wild-type microtubule contacts.
source: Thus, in neither nucleotide state is the N255K construct able to form all three wild-type microtubule contacts.
evidence: The conclusion is based on analysis of the cryo-EM reconstructions of N255K in both nucleotide states.

claim: Microtubule attachment, mediated by the universally conserved 'linchpin' residue N255, triggers a clamshell opening of the nucleotide cleft and accompanying release of ADP.
source: By comparing these models with existing X-ray structures of ADP-bound kinesin, we infer a mechanistic scheme in which microtubule attachment, mediated by a universally conserved 'linchpin' residue in kinesin (N255), triggers a clamshell opening of the nucleotide cleft and accompanying release of ADP.
evidence: The mechanistic scheme is inferred from comparison of the cryo-EM models with X-ray structures.

claim: Binding of ATP re-closes the nucleotide cleft in a manner that tightly couples to translocation of cargo via kinesin's 'neck linker' element.
source: Binding of ATP re-closes the cleft in a manner that tightly couples to translocation of cargo, via kinesin's 'neck linker' element.
evidence: The coupling mechanism is inferred from the structural transitions observed in the cryo-EM models.

claim: The structural transitions in kinesin are reminiscent of the analogous nucleotide-exchange steps in the myosin and F1-ATPase motors.
source: These structural transitions are reminiscent of the analogous nucleotide-exchange steps in the myosin and F1-ATPase motors and inform how the two heads of a kinesin dimer 'gate' each other to promote coordinated stepping along microtubules.
evidence: The comparison is based on structural similarities with other motor proteins.

claim: Conventional kinesin is the founding member of a superfamily of molecular motors that use ATP hydrolysis energy to transport cargo along microtubules.
source: Conventional kinesin is the founding member of a superfamily of molecular motors that use the energy of ATP hydrolysis to transport cargo along microtubules, serving essential roles in a wide variety of cellular processes, most notably mitosis and neuronal transport.
evidence: This is established knowledge about kinesin's function.

claim: More than 20 different members of the kinesin superfamily are identified with mitosis alone.
source: More than 20 different members of the kinesin superfamily are identified with mitosis alone, underscoring the motor's fundamental importance in the cellular life cycle (Rath and Kozielski, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Rath and Kozielski, 2012.

claim: During active motility, the dimerized motor domains of kinesin-1 take alternating, eight nanometer steps toward the microtubule plus end, tracking along single protofilaments.
source: During active motility, the dimerized motor domains take alternating, eight nanometer steps toward the microtubule plus end, tracking along single protofilaments (Gennerich and Vale, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Gennerich and Vale, 2009.

claim: Each kinesin motor domain cycles between conformations that are strongly attached to the microtubule (no-nucleotide and ATP-bound) and ones that are weakly attached (ADP-bound).
source: Underlying this behavior, each motor domain cycles between conformations that are strongly attached to the microtubule (no-nucleotide and ATP-bound) and ones that are weakly attached (ADP-bound).
evidence: This is established knowledge about kinesin's mechanochemical cycle.

claim: Binding of ATP during the microtubule-attached phase causes the neck linker to dock along the side of the motor domain in the plus end direction.
source: Additionally, binding of ATP during the microtubule-attached phase of the motor domain causes a structural element called the neck linker (Figure 1A) to dock along the side of the motor domain in the plus end direction (Rice et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Rice et al., 1999.

claim: Neck linker docking is accompanied by translocation of the cargo and the partner head in the direction of travel.
source: The neck linker connects the C-terminus of the motor domain to the stalk, so that docking is accompanied by translocation of the cargo and the partner in the direction of travel.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural connection between the neck linker and the stalk.

claim: 14-protofilament microtubules outnumbered 13-protofilament by approximately 3:1 in the cryo-EM samples.
source: Multi-reference analysis performed using a range of different microtubule assemblies (12–15 protofilaments) established that 14-protofilament microtubules outnumbered 13-protofilament by approximately 3:1, with only marginal populations of other symmetry forms.
evidence: The ratio is determined from multi-reference analysis of the cryo-EM data.

claim: The final no-nucleotide reconstruction used a total of 10,029 8 nm repeats, for a total of ~140,000 asymmetric units (14 protofilaments).
source: For the final no-nucleotide reconstruction, a total of 10,029 8 nm repeats were used, for a total of ∼140000 asymmetric units (14 protofilaments).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data used in the reconstruction.

claim: The final ADP•Al•Fx reconstruction used a total of 2,394 8 nm repeats, for a total of ~33,600 asymmetric units (14 protofilaments).
source: A total of 2394 8 nm repeats, for a total of ∼33,600 asymmetric units, were used for the final ADP•Al•Fx reconstruction (14 protofilaments).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the data used in the reconstruction.

claim: The extrapolated maximum rate for microtubule-stimulated ADP release for N255K was kmax = 0.26 ± 0.04 s−1, with an apparent microtubule dissociation constant of K0.5 = 21.3 ± 6.3 μΜ.
source: The extrapolated maximum rate for microtubule-stimulated ADP release was kmax = 0.26 ± 0.04 s−1, with an apparent microtubule dissociation constant of K0.5 = 21.3 ± 6.3 μΜ.
evidence: These are measured kinetic parameters from stopped-flow experiments shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: N255 acts as a 'linchpin' that links closure of kinesin's switch loops to interactions at a single site on alpha tubulin.
source: The preceding analysis has indicated that residue N255 in kinesin plays a key role in the motor's microtubule response pathway. In effect, this site appears to act as a 'linchpin' that links closure of kinesin's switch loops to interactions at a single site on alpha tubulin (See Figure 4D–F).
evidence: The linchpin role is inferred from structural analysis shown in Figure 4D-F.

claim: The N255K mutant is incapable of maintaining a fixed orientation on the microtubule surface.
source: On the other hand, the N255K mutant appears to be incapable of maintaining a fixed orientation on the microtubule surface.
evidence: The conclusion is based on cryo-EM analysis showing rotational mobility of the N255K mutant.

claim: Flexibility in the N255K-microtubule contact allows the mutant to maintain affinity for microtubules even when the switch loops are open.
source: Presumably, flexibility in the resulting contact allows the N255K mutant to maintain affinity for microtubules even when the switch loops are open.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the structural and kinetic data for the N255K mutant.

claim: Failure of the N255K mutant to close the switch loops leads to loss of microtubule-stimulated ADP release and catalysis.
source: However, failure of this mutant to close the switch loops under these conditions would lead to the loss of microtubule-stimulated ADP release and catalysis, consistent with experimental measurements.
evidence: The interpretation is consistent with the kinetic measurements shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: Upon microtubule encounter, alpha tubulin engages N255 to stabilize the closed conformation of the switch loops.
source: Upon encountering the microtubule, alpha tubulin engages N255 in order to stabilize the closed conformation of the switch loops.
evidence: This is part of the mechanistic model inferred from the structural data.

claim: The primary consequence of switch loop closure is to revise the mechanical linkages between kinesin's upper subdomain and the other two subdomains.
source: Here, the primary consequence of switch loop closure is to revise the mechanical linkages between kinesin's upper subdomain and the other two subdomains.
evidence: This is part of the mechanistic model inferred from the structural data.

claim: In the detached ADP state, the upper subdomain forms a semi-rigid junction with the N-terminal subdomain via interactions between the open switch II loop and the P-loop.
source: In the detached ADP state of the motor, the upper subdomain forms a semi-rigid junction with the N-terminal subdomain (Figure 8B, top panels), via interactions between the open switch II loop and the P-loop.
evidence: This is part of the mechanistic model shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Upon microtubule attachment, the upper domain trades its junction with the N-terminal subdomain for a new one with the lower subdomain, mediated by the closed switch loops.
source: However, upon microtubule attachment the upper domain trades this junction for a new one with the lower subdomain, mediated by the closed switch loops (Figure 8B, bottom panels).
evidence: This is part of the mechanistic model shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Disengagement of the N-terminal subdomain from the upper subdomain allows the nucleotide cleft to relax into its open state and release ADP.
source: First, disengagement of the N-terminal subdomain from the upper subdomain allows the nucleotide cleft to relax into its open state and release ADP.
evidence: This is part of the mechanistic model inferred from the structural data.

claim: Fixing the upper and lower subdomains together introduces a well-defined allosteric pathway between the neck linker and the nucleotide cleft.
source: Second, fixing the upper and lower subdomains together introduces a well-defined allosteric pathway between the neck linker and the nucleotide cleft, so that closure of the nucleotide cleft by ATP becomes energetically coupled to docking of the neck linker.
evidence: This is part of the mechanistic model inferred from the structural data.

claim: The structure models contrast with a newly published cryo-EM study by Atherton et al. (2014).
source: The structure models presented here contrast with a newly published cryo-EM study of the kinesin-microtubule complex by Atherton et al. (2014).
evidence: This is a direct comparison with another published study.

claim: The no-nucleotide conformation proposed by Atherton et al. exhibits neither an open nucleotide cleft nor twisting between the N-terminal and upper subdomains.
source: However, the no-nucleotide conformation proposed by Atherton et al. seems to exhibit neither an open nucleotide cleft (as defined in the current work) nor twisting between the N-terminal and upper subdomains, both of which are signature traits of our no-nucleotide model.
evidence: This is a comparison with the Atherton et al. study.

claim: The mechanistic scheme proposed by Atherton et al. is starkly different from the one presented in this work.
source: Consequently, the mechanistic scheme proposed by Atherton et al. is starkly different from the one summarized in Figure 8B.
evidence: This is a comparison with the Atherton et al. study.

claim: The improved resolution of the cryo-EM maps (5-6 Å vs 6-7 Å in Atherton et al.) allows resolution of the distinctive hooked shape of the P-loop in the no-nucleotide map.
source: The improved resolution of the cryo-EM maps presented here (5–6 Å vs 6–7 Å in the Atherton et al. study) allows us to resolve the distinctive hooked shape of the P-loop in the no-nucleotide map, precisely defining its position with respect to the switch II loop and thus contributing to our identification of an open conformation of the nucleotide cleft (compare Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1 of the current work with Figure 2 in Atherton et al.).
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of resolution and features between the two studies.

claim: The simulation method used here places more emphasis on a chemically realistic simulation potential by incorporating explicitly represented solvent molecules.
source: Moreover, the simulation method used here to develop all-atom models places more emphasis on a chemically realistic simulation potential, by incorporating explicitly represented solvent molecules and keeping the magnitude of the perturbing cryo-EM potential as small as possible (See 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This describes the methodological approach used in the current work.

claim: Lower resolution, different refinement methods, and additional a priori assumptions in Atherton et al. may have impeded their identification of an open arrangement of the nucleotide cleft.
source: It therefore seems likely that lower resolution, different refinement methods, and also the use of additional a priori assumptions (i.e., fragment selection for the rigid-body fitting) in the methods of the Atherton et al. study may have impeded their identification of an open arrangement of the nucleotide cleft, in their no-nucleotide model.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation comparing methodologies between studies.

claim: The mechanism inferred for kinesin reveals new parallels with the myosin molecular motor.
source: The mechanism inferred here for kinesin reveals new parallels with the myosin molecular motor, which appears to be ancestrally related to kinesin (Kull et al., 1998) and shares very similar nucleotide-sensing 'switch' motifs (Kull et al., 1996; Sablin et al., 1996).
evidence: The parallel is based on structural comparison and is supported by citations.

claim: In myosin, the 'linchpin' asparagine residue interacts natively with a conserved tyrosine within the lower 50kD domain of myosin itself, rather than with the filament.
source: In this light, it is worth noting that the 'linchpin' N255 residue in kinesin is conserved in myosin, but interacts natively with a conserved tyrosine found within the lower 50kD domain of myosin itself, rather than interacting with the filament as occurs with kinesin.
evidence: This is a comparison based on structural knowledge of myosin.

claim: In myosin, the linchpin asparagine holds the switch II loop near its 'closed' conformation even in the absence of actin.
source: Consequently, in myosin this asparagine holds the switch II loop near its 'closed' conformation even in the absence of actin, which could help explain why myosin, unlike kinesin, shows strong catalytic activity even in the absence of its partner filament (Geeves and Holmes, 2005).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural comparison with myosin and is supported by citation.

claim: An X-ray crystal structure of no-nucleotide kinesin in complex with a non-polymerized tubulin dimer published concurrently is in excellent agreement with the model presented here (backbone RMSD 1.28Å).
source: Concurrently with the current work, an X-ray crystal structure of no-nucleotide kinesin in complex with a non-polymerized tubulin dimer has been published (Cao et al., 2014). The structure of no-nucleotide kinesin reported in the X-ray study is in excellent agreement with model presented here (backbone RMSD for all visible residues is 1.28Å).
evidence: The agreement is based on comparison with the Cao et al. 2014 X-ray structure.

claim: The detailed interactions of kinesin and tubulin seen in the Cao et al. X-ray structure are fully consistent with the models and mechanism presented in the current work.
source: Accordingly, the detailed interactions of kinesin and tubulin seen in the X-ray structure appear to be fully consistent with the models and mechanism presented in the current work.
evidence: This is a comparison with the Cao et al. 2014 X-ray structure.
